text:
“How industrious you are, Constance,” he said admiringly. “Always busy—you are so lovely to look at when you sit at your work.”

She did not answer.

“What is it you are knitting now, again?” His tone was modest, yet so interested.

“Stockings.”

“For the poor children?”

“Yes.”

There was a pause.

“Do you know what day it is today, Constance?” Ring asked after clearing his throat a couple of times; his voice was timid and uncertain.

“No,” she said curtly.

“Why, it is the twenty-sixth of October; didn’t you remember?”

“No,” was the answer.

“And I, who thought—” He had almost let the words slip and revealed that he knew her aunt had been there. “I see,” he continued, and smiled in appreciation of his good memory, “so you had forgotten it—our engagement day, Constance,” he added more softly.

“I do not think there is any pleasure in remembering it, for that matter,” she said drily.

Ring sighed deeply.

“Oh no, Constance, you may be right about that, as far as you are concerned. But I—yes, I cannot help regarding it as the happiest day of my life—yes, next to our wedding day, that is.”

“Tsh!” she said, making a gesture of displeasure.

“Yes, yes, Constance, I shall be quiet if that is what you wish, not say a peep that you do not give me leave to say; I shall do everything to please you.” He leaned toward her with an imploring look and spoke softly and timidly.

She turned away with an expression of weariness.

“Oh, Constance, if you could bring yourself, on this day,” he continued, “to give me just one little caress—you would be doing me a kindness.” His voice broke; he covered his eyes with his hand and breathed slowly, almost groaning.

Constance measured him with an attentive glance.

“Now he has surely been drinking again,” she thought.

He rose, walked up and down the floor a couple of times, and then quietly resumed his former seat.

“I have been cherishing a vain hope,” he began again in a distressed tone. “I imagined that the memory of this day might make you more gently disposed. Oh, Constance, you are very, very hard toward me.” He bent forward, rested his elbow on his knee, and his forehead in his hand.

“Tell me one thing,” Constance said coldly. “What did you really mean when you so readily agreed to take me back on the condition I laid down?”

“What I meant,” he stammered, “I meant—”

She looked him straight in the face. He became confused.

“I do not understand you,” he broke off, letting his head sink.

“You acted as though you found it so reasonable, as though it had never even occurred to you that it could be otherwise. Do you remember that?”

“That was sincere on my part too, Constance. I could understand so well that you could not, just at once—. But of course I hoped—” He stopped and sighed.

“There was no question of at once or later, or of any kind of future possibility of change. You agreed fully and unreservedly to my demand. And when I think now of how you behave—” She suddenly broke off. “Good God, that you are not ashamed of yourself,” she added, half turned away.

“I loved you so deeply, Constance,” he groaned.

“Be quiet with that word; it is disgusting to me in your mouth,” she said with flaring anger.

“I could not help believing that time would soften your feelings!” he exclaimed, straightening up in his seat. “I did have a hope that one day I might succeed in winning you back. If that too is to be counted as a crime against me, then—” He stopped.

“You trusted that you would wear me out, so that in the end I would yield; that is why you began pestering me almost at once. You broke your word from the very beginning—there is not a spark of character in you.”

“It is not easy for a man to show character when he is placed as I am. To go and look at you every day, to be so near you and never dare touch you—. Oh, Constance, you must put an end to this; you must become mine again, you must, you must!”

He sank to his knees and hid his face in her dress.

“Get up,” she said with displeasure. “Why are you lying there?”

He obeyed at once and sat back down on the chair.

“Your calculation was not foolish,” she said, looking at him with an almost hateful gaze. “You knew what you were undertaking; more than I did. But I surrender; it is I who have drawn the short straw. There you are, you may have it as you wish—.”

She had risen and now stood with folded arms, staring straight ahead.

He sprang up.

“You will be my wife again as in the old days,” he whispered, holding out his hands toward her. “Oh, Constance”—a melting note entered his voice—“this is too much joy; it comes too suddenly.” He clutched his head. “You forgive me completely, wholly—”

Something resembling laughter interrupted him.

“I do not forgive you—never, do you understand?” She stepped closer. “Beg the corpse of a person you have murdered for forgiveness and see whether it answers you. I am doing it out of self-contempt, do you hear—out of self-contempt! It is the consequence of my defeat, the defeat I suffered when I abandoned the divorce, that I am now taking upon myself.” She clenched her hands and swept past him. “It is no use trying to flee the consequences of one’s actions,” she cried piteously. “They follow at one’s heels and overpower one.” She paced back and forth in the most violent agitation.

“No, Constance, once you came back, it had to end this way; a relationship such as the one you imagined is an impossibility, an unnatural thing. But you shall see, it can still turn out well; I shall yet come to make you happy.” He took a step toward her.

“Happy,” she said with indescribable scorn. “Such terms have no place in a relationship like mine. Let us see the matter as it is.” She suddenly went right up to him. “When I now consent to be your wife,” she said threateningly, “it does not mean what you think! No, I shall tell you something—it would be precisely the same to me if it were any other man whatsoever whom I was to be forced to accept, do you understand, precisely the same.”

Ring involuntarily flinched.

“Oh no, Constance, do not speak so horribly,” he pleaded. “But it does not matter, if only you will become mine again; this is a mood that will pass. Oh, Constance, I could lie on my knees and thank you all night long if I were allowed, but of course you will not have it.”
